title: Unit tests with JUnit
intro: JUnit gives you a standard way to test Java code automatically, while AssertJ makes the assertions readable and Mockito helps isolate a unit from its dependencies. In this lesson, you will build focused tests for a Spring service and learn how to catch subtle regressions rather than merely execute code.
body:
## Your first JUnit test

**JUnit 5** is the testing framework commonly used for Java applications. Spring Boot's test starter brings JUnit together with other useful testing tools.

For a typical Spring Boot project, you can use:

~~~xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
~~~

The Spring Boot test starter includes JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito, and other testing support.

A **unit test** should normally test one small unit of behaviour without starting the whole application or connecting to a real database.

Imagine the task manager has a `TaskService` with a method that creates a task. A first test might look like:

~~~java
class TaskServiceTest {

    @Test
    void createsTaskWithTitle() {
        Task task = service.create("Learn testing");

        assertThat(task.getTitle()).isEqualTo("Learn testing");
    }
}
~~~

The test method describes a behaviour: creating a task results in the expected title.

## @Test, @DisplayName, and @BeforeEach

`@Test` tells JUnit that a method is a test.

`@DisplayName` lets you provide a human-readable name. This can make test output much easier to understand:

~~~java
@Test
@DisplayName("creates a task with the supplied title")
void createsTaskWithTitle() {
    // ...
}
~~~

`@BeforeEach` runs before every test method in the class. It is useful for creating fresh test state:

~~~java
@BeforeEach
void setUp() {
    repository = mock(TaskRepository.class);
    service = new TaskService(repository);
}
~~~

The fact that it runs before **each** test is important. Tests should not accidentally share mutable state.

If five tests use a fresh service, `setUp()` runs five times.

## AssertJ assertions

JUnit can perform assertions, but Spring Boot's test starter also includes **AssertJ**, which provides a fluent assertion API.

A fluent API lets you express an assertion in a chain that reads almost like a sentence:

~~~java
assertThat(task.getTitle()).isEqualTo("Learn testing");
~~~

You can test collections with `hasSize`:

~~~java
assertThat(tasks).hasSize(3);
~~~

You can also extract a property from objects in a collection:

~~~java
assertThat(tasks)
    .extracting(Task::getTitle)
    .containsExactly("Learn Java", "Learn Spring");
~~~

This checks the values that matter without requiring you to write a separate assertion for every object.

Other useful AssertJ assertions include `isTrue()`, `isFalse()`, `isNull()`, `isNotNull()`, `contains()`, and `startsWith()`.

Choose assertions that communicate the expected behaviour clearly.

## Testing exceptions

Exceptions are part of application behaviour too.

Suppose creating a task with an empty title should fail. You can test that with AssertJ's `assertThatThrownBy`:

~~~java
assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.create(""))
    .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
    .hasMessage("Title is required");
~~~

The lambda contains the operation that is expected to throw.

This is better than wrapping the entire test in a broad try/catch because the assertion clearly states what exception is expected and can verify its message as well.

Keep the operation that should throw inside the assertion. Otherwise, you may accidentally test the wrong part of the setup.

## Parameterized tests

Sometimes the same behaviour needs to be tested with several inputs.

Writing separate methods for every input can become repetitive. JUnit provides **parameterized tests** for this situation.

For example:

~~~java
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({
    "0, 0",
    "1, 1",
    "10, 10"
})
void returnsExpectedValue(int input, int expected) {
    assertThat(service.calculate(input)).isEqualTo(expected);
}
~~~

`@ParameterizedTest` tells JUnit to execute the test multiple times.

`@CsvSource` supplies comma-separated values for each invocation.

Parameterized tests are particularly useful for boundaries and validation rules.

For example, if an employee receives a discount after a certain number of loyalty years, test the values around the boundary:

~~~text
2 years -> normal rule
3 years -> discounted rule
4 years -> discounted rule
~~~

Boundary tests are excellent at catching off-by-one errors.

## Mocking a repository with Mockito

A service often depends on another component. Our `TaskService` might depend on `TaskRepository`.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Testing a service in isolation", "nodes": [{"id": "t", "label": "TaskServiceTest", "kind": "code"}, {"id": "s", "label": "TaskService", "sub": "real object under test", "highlight": true}, {"id": "m", "label": "@Mock TaskRepository", "sub": "when(…).thenReturn(…)"}, {"id": "v", "label": "assertThat / verify", "kind": "code"}], "edges": [{"from": "t", "to": "s", "label": "calls"}, {"from": "s", "to": "m", "label": "uses"}, {"from": "s", "to": "v", "label": "result"}]}
~~~

If you are writing a unit test for the service, you usually do not need a real database. You can replace the repository with a **mock**.

Mockito is a library for creating and configuring such test doubles.

Create a mock with:

~~~java
TaskRepository repository = mock(TaskRepository.class);
~~~

Then configure its behaviour with `when(...).thenReturn(...)`:

~~~java
when(repository.findById(42L))
    .thenReturn(Optional.of(task));
~~~

Now the service can call `findById(42L)` and receive the controlled test object.

You can also verify that an interaction happened:

~~~java
verify(repository).findById(42L);
~~~

A typical test might therefore look like:

~~~java
@Test
void returnsTaskFromRepository() {
    Task task = new Task(42L, "Learn JUnit");
    when(repository.findById(42L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(task));

    Task result = service.findById(42L);

    assertThat(result.getTitle()).isEqualTo("Learn JUnit");
    verify(repository).findById(42L);
}
~~~

The assertion verifies the result. The `verify` assertion checks an interaction that is meaningful to this behaviour.

## When a fake is better than a mock

A **fake** is a simple working implementation of a dependency designed for tests.

For example, you could create an in-memory task repository using a `Map<Long, Task>`.

A fake can sometimes be easier to understand than a large collection of Mockito expectations.

Use a mock when you need to control a dependency's response or verify an important interaction. Prefer a simple fake when the fake naturally models the dependency and makes the test easier to understand.

Do not mock everything automatically.

If every test contains many `when()` and `verify()` calls, the tests can become coupled to implementation details rather than behaviour.

## Naming tests by behaviour

Test names should explain what the application is supposed to do.

Prefer:

~~~text
returns 404 when task does not exist
rejects a task with an empty title
allows an owner to update their task
applies the employee discount
~~~

Avoid vague names such as:

~~~text
testTask
works
serviceTest
checkStuff
~~~

A good test name becomes especially useful when CI reports a failure at 2 AM. You should be able to understand the failed behaviour without immediately opening the implementation.

A test name should answer something close to:

~~~text
Given this situation, what should happen?
~~~

## Testing business rules

Unit tests are particularly valuable for business rules because they can cover many cases very quickly.

Imagine a pricing rule:

~~~text
Employee -> 30% discount
10+ loyalty years -> 15% discount
3–9 loyalty years -> 10% discount
Otherwise -> no discount
Negative price -> error
Result -> never below zero and rounded to 2 decimals
~~~

A weak test might check only one normal case:

~~~java
assertThat(priceWithDiscount(100, customer)).isEqualTo(100);
~~~

A stronger test suite checks boundaries and exceptional cases too.

For the three-year boundary, test both sides:

~~~text
2 years -> no loyalty discount
3 years -> 10% discount
~~~

For ten years:

~~~text
9 years -> 10% discount
10 years -> 15% discount
~~~

This style of testing is useful because small implementation mistakes often occur exactly at boundaries.

## Mutation testing mindset

There is an interesting way to evaluate whether tests are actually useful: imagine deliberately changing the implementation in a small way.

This is the basic idea behind **mutation testing**. A mutation testing tool changes code in controlled ways, such as changing `>=` to `>` or removing an operation. Your tests should fail when the behaviour becomes incorrect.

For example, suppose the rule says three or more loyalty years receive a discount:

~~~java
loyaltyYears >= 3
~~~

A subtle bug would be:

~~~java
loyaltyYears > 3
~~~

A test that only checks ten years would still pass. A test for exactly three years catches the mutation.

This is why a test suite should not simply execute many lines of code. It should challenge the important decisions in the implementation.

The exercise in this lesson uses this idea directly. You will write a test suite that receives an implementation and must reject several subtly broken versions.

## Running tests in IntelliJ IDEA Community

IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition can run Maven and JUnit tests without requiring the paid edition.

~~~callout ide Run tests from the gutter
Click the green ▶ next to a test method or class, or press **Ctrl+Shift+F10** (macOS: **⌃⇧R**) with the cursor inside. Failed tests show a diff — click **<Click to see difference>** to compare expected and actual values side by side.
~~~

When IntelliJ recognizes a JUnit test class, you can usually run a test or test class using the gutter icons next to the test methods and class.

You can also right-click the test class or method and choose the appropriate run action.

After a failure, IntelliJ shows the failed assertion and the relevant stack trace. You can re-run failed tests from the test runner rather than executing the entire suite manually.

A practical workflow is:

~~~text
Write test
   ↓
Run test
   ↓
Read failure
   ↓
Fix implementation or test
   ↓
Re-run failed tests
~~~

When the test suite is larger, you can still run individual tests during development and the complete suite before committing.

## Running tests with Maven

Your project can also run tests without the IDE:

~~~shell
./mvnw test
~~~

The Maven Wrapper, `mvnw`, lets the project use its configured Maven version without requiring you to install a matching Maven version globally.

On Windows, the wrapper command is commonly:

~~~shell
mvnw.cmd test
~~~

Running tests from the command line is important because CI will normally execute commands rather than interact with your IDE.

If IntelliJ says everything is green but `./mvnw test` fails, investigate the difference. The command-line build is an important representation of what automated CI will execute.

## Common mistakes

### Testing only the happy path

A single successful example rarely covers a business rule completely. Test invalid input, boundaries, and important alternative cases.

### Mocking every dependency

Mocks can make unit tests fast, but excessive mocking creates brittle tests that verify implementation details. Consider whether a simple fake or integration test would communicate the behaviour better.

### Ignoring boundaries

Rules such as “three or more” and “ten or more” should be tested at exactly three and exactly ten, as well as just below those values.

### Writing vague test names

When a test fails, its name should tell you what behaviour broke. Avoid names such as `test1()` or `worksCorrectly()`.

### Testing implementation instead of behaviour

If changing an internal method name breaks ten tests even though the application's behaviour is unchanged, those tests may be too tightly coupled to implementation details.

### Assuming green means complete

A passing suite only means that the behaviours covered by those tests currently pass. Missing tests can leave important bugs undetected.

## A practical unit-testing workflow

For each important piece of business logic, start by identifying the behaviour you want to guarantee.

Then consider the normal case, invalid inputs, boundaries, and important alternatives.

For a service that depends on a repository, decide whether a mock, fake, or integration test provides the clearest test.

A useful workflow is:

~~~text
Identify behaviour
      ↓
Choose important examples
      ↓
Add boundary and error cases
      ↓
Arrange
      ↓
Act
      ↓
Assert
      ↓
Run locally
      ↓
Run ./mvnw test
      ↓
CI runs the same tests
~~~

Good unit tests should make your code easier to change. If you refactor the internal implementation but preserve the behaviour, most of the tests should continue to pass.

That is the real value of unit testing: not a large number of green checkmarks, but reliable feedback about whether your application still behaves as intended.
takeaways: Spring Boot's test starter provides JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito, and other tools for practical Java testing.
Use AssertJ to write readable assertions and parameterized tests to cover multiple inputs and important boundaries.
Mockito can isolate a service from a repository, but simple fakes are sometimes clearer than heavily mocked tests.
Name tests after the behaviour they guarantee and include invalid inputs and boundary cases.
Run tests both from IntelliJ IDEA Community and with ./mvnw test so the same suite can run reliably in CI.

quiz.question: What does @Test tell JUnit?
options: That a method should be treated as a test
That a method should be exposed as a REST endpoint
That a method should connect to PostgreSQL
That a method should always run before every other test
quiz.explanation: @Test marks a method as a JUnit test method so the test runner can discover and execute it.

quiz.question: What is a useful purpose of @BeforeEach?
options: It runs only when the complete test suite passes
It creates fresh setup before each test method
It converts unit tests into E2E tests
It disables Mockito
quiz.explanation: @BeforeEach runs before every test method, making it useful for creating fresh and independent test state.

quiz.question: What does Mockito's when(...).thenReturn(...) do?
options: It permanently changes the production repository
It runs the test twice
It configures a mock to return a specified value for a matching call
It verifies that a method was called
quiz.explanation: when(...).thenReturn(...) defines the behaviour of a Mockito mock when the configured method call occurs. verify(...) is used to check interactions.

quiz.question: Why is testing exactly three loyalty years important when the rule is '3 or more'?
options: It makes Mockito faster
It guarantees 100% code coverage
It prevents all SQL injection attacks
It checks the boundary where the rule changes and can catch an off-by-one error
quiz.explanation: Boundary values are where conditions such as >= 3 are easily implemented incorrectly as > 3. Testing exactly three can expose that subtle bug.

quiz.question: Which command runs the Maven test suite using the project's Maven Wrapper?
options: ./mvnw test
npm test
java test
spring test --all
quiz.explanation: ./mvnw test runs the Maven test phase using the Maven Wrapper configured by the project.

exercise.title: Catch broken implementations
exercise.task: Write `runSuite(fn)` as a small mutation-testing-style test suite. The supplied implementation `fn` has the signature `fn(price, customer)` where `customer` is `{ loyaltyYears: number, isEmployee: boolean }`. The correct rules are: employees receive 30% off; otherwise customers with 10 or more loyalty years receive 15% off; otherwise customers with 3 or more loyalty years receive 10% off; the result must never be below 0; the result is rounded to 2 decimal places; and a negative or non-finite price must throw `Error("Invalid price")`. Your `runSuite(fn)` must run your own assertions against the supplied `fn` and return `true` only when every assertion passes. It must use only the `fn` parameter and must never call or inspect the global `priceWithDiscount` function. Your suite must be strong enough to return `true` for the correct implementation and `false` for each of these four subtly broken implementations: one uses the wrong boundary for 3 loyalty years, one forgets rounding, one ignores the employee discount, and one accepts a negative price instead of throwing. Include tests for the important boundaries, employee behaviour, rounding, invalid prices, non-finite prices, and the non-negative result rule.
exercise.hint: Think like a mutation tester: every important rule needs at least one assertion that would fail if that rule were subtly changed. In particular, test exactly 3 and exactly 10 loyalty years, an employee with and without loyalty years, a value such as 19.99 that requires rounding after a discount, and negative, Infinity, and NaN inputs. Catch exceptions inside runSuite and return false when any assertion fails.

tests.name: The correct implementation passes the suite
It catches the three-year boundary bug
tests.code: function broken(price, customer) { if (!Number.isFinite(price) || price < 0) throw new Error("Invalid price"); let discount = 0; if (customer.isEmployee) discount = 0.30; else if (customer.loyaltyYears >= 10) discount = 0.15; else if (customer.loyaltyYears > 3) discount = 0.10; const result = Math.max(0, price * (1 - discount)); return Math.round(result * 100) / 100; } return runSuite(broken) === false;

tests.name: It catches the missing rounding bug
tests.code: function broken(price, customer) { if (!Number.isFinite(price) || price < 0) throw new Error("Invalid price"); let discount = 0; if (customer.isEmployee) discount = 0.30; else if (customer.loyaltyYears >= 10) discount = 0.15; else if (customer.loyaltyYears >= 3) discount = 0.10; return Math.max(0, price * (1 - discount)); } return runSuite(broken) === false;

tests.name: It catches the employee discount bug
tests.code: function broken(price, customer) { if (!Number.isFinite(price) || price < 0) throw new Error("Invalid price"); let discount = 0; if (!customer.isEmployee && customer.loyaltyYears >= 10) discount = 0.15; else if (!customer.isEmployee && customer.loyaltyYears >= 3) discount = 0.10; const result = Math.max(0, price * (1 - discount)); return Math.round(result * 100) / 100; } return runSuite(broken) === false;

tests.name: It catches the negative price bug
tests.code: function broken(price, customer) { let discount = 0; if (customer.isEmployee) discount = 0.30; else if (customer.loyaltyYears >= 10) discount = 0.15; else if (customer.loyaltyYears >= 3) discount = 0.10; const result = Math.max(0, price * (1 - discount)); return Math.round(result * 100) / 100; } return runSuite(broken) === false;

tests.name: It catches missing non-finite validation
tests.code: function broken(price, customer) { if (price < 0) throw new Error("Invalid price"); let discount = 0; if (customer.isEmployee) discount = 0.30; else if (customer.loyaltyYears >= 10) discount = 0.15; else if (customer.loyaltyYears >= 3) discount = 0.10; const result = Math.max(0, price * (1 - discount)); return Math.round(result * 100) / 100; } return runSuite(broken) === false;

tests.name: It uses the supplied function instead of the global function
tests.code: function alwaysWrong() { return -999; } return runSuite(alwaysWrong) === false;
